ai.definition: A blockchain-based supply chain management system utilizes distributed ledger technology to record transactions across a network of computers, ensuring transparency, security, and immutability of data throughout the supply chain.
ai.howItWorks: Data about products and their movements are recorded on a blockchain. Each transaction is verified by multiple nodes in the network before being added to the immutable ledger. This process ensures that all parties have access to the same up-to-date information, reducing discrepancies and increasing trust among participants.
ai.problemSolved: It addresses issues such as lack of transparency, fraud, counterfeiting, and inefficiencies in traditional supply chain management systems by providing a secure, transparent, and tamper-proof record-keeping mechanism.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves developing smart contracts for automated execution of transactions, setting up nodes on the blockchain network, and integrating with existing supply chain systems. This requires significant initial investment in technology infrastructure and skilled personnel.
ai.buildProcess: Developing a blockchain-based system includes defining use cases, selecting appropriate blockchain platforms (e.g., Ethereum, Hyperledger), designing smart contracts, testing the system for security vulnerabilities, and deploying it across the supply chain network.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include initial infrastructure setup, maintenance of nodes, integration with legacy systems, ongoing development costs, and potential regulatory compliance expenses.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is gaining traction in pilot projects but faces challenges in widespread adoption due to complexity, interoperability issues, and the need for standardization.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks are still evolving. There may be concerns around data privacy, jurisdictional issues, and compliance with existing trade regulations.
ai.risks: Technical risks include security breaches, network downtime, and potential centralization of power among dominant nodes. Business risks involve resistance to change from traditional supply chain stakeholders and the need for continuous support and maintenance.
ai.profitability: Profitability is variable depending on the specific application and market segment. Early adopters in high-value industries may see significant benefits, but broader adoption requires overcoming barriers such as cost and complexity.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments could include improvements in scalability, interoperability between different blockchain networks, and integration with other emerging technologies like IoT for real-time tracking.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and continuous node operation. Energy consumption can be managed through optimization techniques such as proof-of-stake mechanisms instead of proof-of-work.

glossary.def: A decentralized, digital ledger that records transactions across multiple computers so that any involved record cannot be altered retroactively.
Automated contracts stored on a blockchain that execute when certain conditions are met, ensuring the trustless and transparent execution of agreements between parties.
A type of database that is managed by multiple participants in a network rather than by a single entity, providing transparency and security for transactions.
